# MDR Software Classification: tablet infusion-pump control app

**Intended purpose (as stated):** "to set and adjust the delivery rate of the [X] infusion pump under clinician control."
**Qualified as a device:** treated as established (you're presenting it as software controlling your own Class III pump). Art. 2(1) qualification is outside what I verify — if it isn't formally settled in your documentation, that's the prior question.

## Class: III

**Route:** 3.3 → same class as the driven device. Rule 11 is never reached.

## Reasoning

| Step | Question | Answer | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | Intended purpose governs, not capability | "to set and adjust the delivery rate of the [X] infusion pump under clinician control" | `[verified]` |
| 3.3 | Drives or influences another device? | **Yes** — setting and adjusting the delivery rate is driving the pump. Class follows the pump: **III** | `[verified]` |
| Rule 11 | Which limb | **Not reached.** 3.3 runs first and disposes of it | `[verified]` |
| Rule 11 | Escalation | n/a | `[verified]` |
| 3.5 | Could a stricter rule apply? | No — III is the highest class, so nothing can raise it | `[verified]` |

The "it doesn't diagnose anything" point is a Rule 11 limb-1 argument, and it's correct as far as it goes — but it never gets used. 3.3 says software that drives a device *falls within the same class as the device*, whatever Rule 11 would have produced on its own. The diagnostic/non-diagnostic question only matters for *independent* software.

The rate display is the one part that, alone, would be independent software (displaying device output without driving it). But it isn't alone: the same app sets the rate, and the intended purpose you've stated is the setting-and-adjusting purpose. Under 3.5 the stricter result governs the device anyway.

"Under clinician control" doesn't change the 3.3 call either. A human in the loop confirming each change doesn't stop the software from being the thing that sets the parameter on the pump.

## What would change this

- **The app stops setting the rate.** A pure read-only display or logging app, with no ability to set or adjust any pump parameter and no gating of alarms, would plausibly be independent under 3.3 and then classified in its own right under Rule 11. That is a product change, not a documentation change.
- **The pump's class.** Class III is inherited from the pump. If the pump's own classification were ever revised, the app's follows it.
- **The intended purpose being stated differently.** If your technical documentation words it more narrowly than the app can actually do, that's a problem with the stated purpose rather than a lower class — 3.1 anchors to intended purpose, but a mismatch between purpose and capability is its own finding.

## Practical consequence worth naming

Class III is your pump's route, and the app now sits on it: notified-body involvement, Annex IX-type assessment depth, clinical evaluation expectations. Whether the app is documented as part of the pump's technical documentation or as a separate device with its own certificate is a structuring decision — either way it doesn't land in Class I, and a "Class I self-certified companion app" plan won't survive.

## Before treating this as settled

This is the Annex VIII text applied to the intended purpose as you stated it. The class drives your conformity route, whether you need a notified body, and the depth of your technical documentation, so confirm it with your regulatory lead or notified body before building on it. The three things to put in front of them:

1. **The 3.3 call** — that setting and adjusting the delivery rate is "driving" the pump, so the app inherits Class III.
2. **That Rule 11 is not reached** — and therefore the absence of a diagnostic function doesn't lower the class.
3. **Whether the app is documented within the pump's technical documentation or as a device in its own right** — a 3.2/3.3 structuring question, not a class question.

## Limits

> This classifies software under MDR Annex VIII implementing rules 3.1–3.7 and Rule 11, retrieved verbatim from EUR-Lex on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover Art. 2(1) qualification, Rules 1–10 or 12–22, Annex XVI, IVDR, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, or national interpretation. Rule 11 is a floor: under 3.5 a stricter rule this skill does not carry may raise the class. A structured first pass and an audit aid, not legal or regulatory advice, and not a substitute for your notified body or a qualified regulatory professional.

## Short answer: Class III.

The relevant provision isn't Rule 11 — it's **Annex VIII, Chapter II, implementing Rule 3.3**:

> "Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device."

Your app sets and adjusts the delivery rate. That is the textbook case of software driving a device. The pump is Class III, so the app is Class III. MDCG 2019-11 uses almost exactly this example (software controlling an infusion pump) and lands in the same place.

## Why the "it doesn't diagnose" reasoning doesn't help you

Three intuitions that commonly lead teams to under-classify here, and why none of them apply:

- **"It's not diagnostic/decision-support, so Rule 11 gives a low class."** Rule 11 covers software that provides *information* used for decisions. Yours doesn't inform a decision, it executes therapy. Rule 3.3 applies instead. And even if you argued both applied, Rule 3.5 says the highest class wins.
- **"It's under clinician control."** A clinician in the loop can matter for Rule 11-style classification, where the human is the one acting on the output. It does nothing under Rule 3.3 — the clinician sets a number, your software is what actually commands the pump. A mis-scaled unit conversion or a stuck UI value causes an overdose regardless of who typed it.
- **"It only displays the current rate, so it's basically a viewer."** The display is a safety-relevant function, not a passive readout. If it shows a rate that doesn't match what the pump is delivering, that's a hazardous situation on its own.

## The one real decision you need to make

Is the app a **part/component of the pump** or a **separately-placed-on-market accessory**? Class III either way, but the regulatory packaging differs:

- **Component** (shipped as part of the pump system, same intended purpose, covered by the pump's certificate): no separate CE marking, no separate UDI-DI, no separate technical documentation. It lives inside the pump's Annex IX file. If the tablet app is the *only* way to set the rate, this is almost certainly the honest characterization, and it's the simpler path.
- **Accessory placed on the market in its own right** (e.g. downloadable, sold independently, works across pump models): classified in its own right per implementing Rule 3.2, still Class III via 3.3 — meaning its own Annex IX conformity assessment, own UDI, own SSCP, own clinical evaluation.

Pick one deliberately and document the rationale; notified bodies push on exactly this point.

## What Class III pulls in

- **Conformity assessment**: Annex IX (QMS + technical documentation assessment) or Annex X + XI. Notified body involvement either way. No Art. 54 scrutiny procedure — that's only for Class III *implantables*.
- **Art. 61 clinical evaluation**, with clinical investigation the default expectation for Class III unless you can justify equivalence.
- **Art. 32 SSCP**, plus PMCF under Annex XIV Part B and annual PSUR.
- **IEC 62304 safety class** — separate axis from the MDR class, but expect **Class C** here (software failure can contribute to death/serious injury via over-infusion). Hardware-side independent protection in the pump — rate limiters, max-dose ceilings, a watchdog on the command channel that the tablet cannot bypass — is the standard way to argue the app's software safety class down. Worth doing for its own sake, but it won't move the MDR class.
- **Tablet platform**: since the app runs on general-purpose hardware, you need IEC 82304-1 thinking plus IEC 60601-1 Clause 16 if the tablet is part of a medical electrical system. Specify minimum platform requirements, OS versions, and what happens on OS updates. Also MDCG 2019-16 for the wireless command channel — the link between tablet and pump is a safety interface, not just an IT interface.

One caveat: this is my read of the classification rules, not a substitute for your regulatory lead or a notified body's opinion — particularly on the component-vs-accessory question, where the right answer depends on commercial facts I don't have.

graders.evidence:
## Class III — and it's not a Rule 11 question

The controlling provision is **Annex VIII, Chapter II, implementing rule 3.5** (MDR 2017/745):

> "Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device. If the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right."

Your app sets and adjusts the delivery rate — that is the definition of *driving* the device. So it inherits the pump's class: **Class III**.

**Why the things you mentioned don't move it:**

- *"Doesn't diagnose anything"* — irrelevant. Rule 3.5 turns on driving/influencing, not on diagnostic function.
- *"Under clinician control"* — a human in the loop doesn't lower the class. It matters for your risk controls and usability engineering (IEC 62366-1), not classification.
- *"Shows the current rate"* — a display function alongside the control function doesn't pull you out of 3.5.
- **Rule 11 is a red herring.** Rule 11 applies to MDSW that is *independent of any other device* and provides information for decisions or monitors physiological parameters. Yours isn't independent. And even if you ran the Rule 11 analysis and landed at IIa/IIb, implementing rule 3.2 (highest applicable class wins) means 3.5 still governs.
- **Calling it an accessory doesn't help either.** Accessories are normally classified in their own right, but 3.5 is the specific rule for driving software and it points straight at the pump's class. MDCG 2019-11 says the same.
- The tablet being general-purpose hardware doesn't change it — though if you *supply or specify* the tablet, the hardware and OS become part of your device definition and you own configuration control over them.

## One thing worth double-checking

You've asserted the pump is Class III, and your app's class is inherited wholesale from that — so it's worth confirming the pump's classification is right. Most volumetric and syringe infusion pumps are **Class IIb** under Rule 12. Class III usually comes from something specific: Rule 14 (incorporates a medicinal substance), or Rule 22 (closed-loop system with an integrated diagnostic function that significantly determines patient management). If the pump is actually IIb, your app is IIb. If your app closes a loop with sensor data, that could itself be what pushes the *system* to III.

## The real decision: separate device or part of the pump?

This matters more than the classification, because the classification is the same either way:

- **Part of the pump device** — same intended purpose, inside the pump's technical documentation, covered by the pump's certificate and UDI as "software as part of a device." Usually the cleaner route if the app only works with your pump, and it avoids a second set of registrations.
- **Device in its own right** — its own CE marking, own Basic UDI-DI, its own Class III certificate and Annex II/III technical documentation.

Either way you're in Annex IX (full QMS plus per-device technical documentation assessment, since Class III gets device-by-device review) or Annex X+XI, with notified body involvement. Class III also brings: clinical investigation expectation under Art. 61(4) — though Art. 61(6)(b) equivalence to your own already-marketed device is plausibly available here; SSCP under Art. 32; annual PSUR; PMCF.

## Don't confuse this with your IEC 62304 class

These are separate axes, and people conflate them because both are called "class."

Your software safety class is most likely **C** — a software failure that commands the wrong rate leads to death or serious injury. This is the one place where "the clinician is in control" and "the pump has its own limits" can actually earn you something: if the pump independently enforces hard rate/dose/volume limits in a channel that doesn't depend on the tablet, you may be able to argue down to Class B via external risk control measures per 62304 §4.3. That architecture — safety limits enforced in the pump, not in the app — is also exactly what a notified body will want to see, and it's worth designing for now rather than retrofitting.

Relevant reading: MDCG 2019-11 (qualification and classification of software), MDCG 2019-16 (cybersecurity), IEC 81001-5-1 if there's any wireless link between tablet and pump.

Worth running past your RA lead and confirming with your notified body, particularly the "part of the pump vs. standalone device" framing — that's the one where their preference has real downstream consequences for your submission.

graders.evidence:
Short answer: **Class III**, on the assumption your pump really is Class III.

## The rule that decides it

MDR **Annex VIII, Chapter II, Implementing Rule 3.3**:

> "Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device. If the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right."

Setting and adjusting the delivery rate is the textbook case of *driving* a device — not merely "influencing" it. So your app inherits the pump's class. MDCG 2019-11 §3.3 confirms this reading and is explicit that **Rule 11 does not apply** here: Rule 11 is for software that is independent of any other device. Your app isn't, so you never get to the "does it provide information used for diagnostic/therapeutic decisions" analysis at all.

Three things that feel like they should lower the class but don't:

- **"It doesn't diagnose."** Irrelevant under 3.3 — that language belongs to Rule 11.
- **"Under clinician control."** No human-in-the-loop discount exists in 3.3. A clinician entering the wrong rate into an app that faithfully transmits it is exactly the hazard being classified.
- **"It's just a UI; the pump enforces its own limits."** Your risk analysis can credit those limits, but classification is driven by intended purpose, not by mitigations.

## The one thing worth verifying

Class III is unusual for an infusion pump. **Rule 12** (devices administering medicinal products) gives Class IIa, or **IIb** where the method of administration is potentially hazardous — which is where most infusion pumps land. Class III normally arrives via **Rule 14** (incorporates an ancillary medicinal substance) or a specific application like direct CNS/cardiovascular delivery.

So confirm *why* the pump is Class III before building a Class III programme around the app. If the pump is actually IIb, the app is IIb — a materially different conformity assessment route. Check the pump's existing classification rationale and certificate.

## Consequence you should decide on now: component or accessory?

This affects your documentation structure more than the class does.

- **Component of the pump system** — same manufacturer, covered by the pump's intended purpose, released and versioned with it. It goes into the *pump's* technical documentation; no separate CE mark or Basic UDI-DI. Usually the cleaner path, but every app update touches a Class III file and your notified body's change-notification rules.
- **Accessory placed on the market in its own right** — separately distributed (app store, separate ordering), its own tech doc, CE mark, Basic UDI-DI, and Annex IX assessment. Per Article 51(1) accessories are classified in their own right, but Rule 3.3 still lands it at the pump's class.

Either way, the tablet itself stays general-purpose hardware — but you own the platform requirements: Annex I §17.3–17.4 (software on a computing platform you don't control), MDCG 2019-16 cybersecurity, and a defined minimum spec / OS version policy. Also worth confirming: IEC 62304 software safety class (almost certainly **Class C** given the hazard), IEC 62366-1 usability with the rate-entry task as your primary safety-related task, and IEC 60601-2-24 alarm/interface obligations if the app presents pump state.

I'm giving you the regulatory reasoning, not a regulatory sign-off — run the component-vs-accessory decision and the pump's Class III basis past your RA/QA lead and your notified body before it hardens into your technical documentation.

## Bottom line: **Class III, Rule 11** (Annex VIII, MDR 2017/745)

### Qualification first

- **It's a medical device.** Article 2(1) — software with an intended purpose of diagnosis/prediction in relation to disease. Confirmed by the MDCG 2019-11 decision steps: it performs an action on data beyond storage, archival, communication or simple search (it analyses images and produces a finding), and it does so for the benefit of individual patients.
- **MDR, not IVDR.** CTA images are not specimens derived from the human body, so Rule 11 of the MDR applies, not the IVDR classification rules.
- **MDSW in its own right, not an accessory.** Your "no connection to any other device" point matters here: it means Annex VIII implementing rule 3.3 (software driving or influencing a device takes that device's class) doesn't apply, and neither does Rule 22 (active therapeutic devices with an integrated closed-loop diagnostic function). Rule 11 is the operative rule, applied to the software standalone.

### Rule 11, first indent

> *Software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes is classified as class IIa, except if such decisions have an impact that may cause: — death or an irreversible deterioration of a person's state of health, in which case it is in class III; or — a serious deterioration of a person's state of health or a surgical intervention, in which case it is classified as class IIb.*

Your intended purpose puts you squarely in the first limb: the output is information used to take a decision with a **therapeutic** purpose (proceed to thrombectomy, or not). So the floor is IIa, and the question is only how far the impact escalates it.

Work the error modes:

- **False negative** (LVO missed or not flagged) → thrombectomy not performed, or performed outside the window → large-territory infarct. That is **death or irreversible deterioration**, not merely serious deterioration. Class III.
- **False positive** → an unnecessary endovascular procedure. That alone is a "surgical intervention" and would carry Class IIb, with a realistic tail of vessel dissection, perforation or haemorrhage that again reaches death/irreversible harm.

The worst credible impact drives the class, so the false-negative path lands you in **Class III**. This is also where MDCG 2019-11's overlay of the IMDRF significance/criticality matrix points: "treat or diagnose" information in a **critical** healthcare situation is the top category, and acute LVO stroke is the textbook critical situation — time-dependent, irreversible, high mortality.

### The Class IIb argument, and why your wording defeats it

The standard argument for IIb on triage software is: *the neurointerventionalist reads the CTA anyway, so the software doesn't drive the decision — it only reorders a worklist or fires a notification.* Some LVO-notification products have been positioned that way.

That argument isn't available to you as written. Your intended purpose says the output is "to support **the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy**." You have explicitly claimed the therapeutic decision, and classification follows the intended purpose you state, not the residual risk you believe your human-in-the-loop mitigations achieve. Risk controls affect your risk management file; they don't pull you down a class.

If you genuinely intend a lower-claim product, the change has to be real, not cosmetic: a pure prioritisation/notification claim, no diagnostic output rendered to the user, no LVO "flag" presented as a finding, and labelling stating it is not for diagnostic use and not to be relied on for treatment decisions. Expect a notified body to test that hard against your UI, marketing and clinical evaluation — and note that even then, in stroke, changing time-to-treatment is itself outcome-determining, so IIb is the realistic floor rather than IIa. My recommendation: don't contort the claim. Take Class III and build the evidence for the claim you actually want to make.

### What Class III commits you to

- **Conformity assessment:** Annex IX Chapters I *and* II — full QMS audit **plus** notified body assessment of the technical documentation for **this device** (not the Class IIb sampling regime). Alternatively Annex X + XI Part A.
- **Clinical investigation:** Article 61(4) — required for Class III devices unless you can rely on the narrow equivalence route to a device already marketed by you (Art. 61(4)–(5)) or the legacy-data exemption in 61(6). For a novel algorithm, assume a prospective investigation, plus a pre-specified standalone performance study against an adjudicated reference standard.
- **SSCP:** Article 32 Summary of Safety and Clinical Performance required, validated by the NB and published in Eudamed.
- **PSUR:** annual, submitted to the NB via Eudamed (Art. 86), with a robust PMCF plan.
- **Not** subject to the Article 54 clinical evaluation consultation procedure — that's limited to Class III *implantables* and certain Class IIb active devices, so a non-implantable Class III SaMD escapes the expert panel step.
- Standards to build to: ISO 14971, IEC 62304 (Class III device use case almost certainly software safety class C), IEC 82304-1, ISO 13485, plus IEC 62366-1 — human factors will be scrutinised heavily given the decision-support framing.

### One flag

If the analysis is ML-based, Class III triggers third-party conformity assessment under MDR, which makes it a **high-risk AI system** under Article 6(1) of the AI Act (Annex I route). Those obligations bite from **2 August 2027**, so they are inside the window of a programme starting now. Plan a combined MDR/AI Act technical file — data governance, logging, transparency and human oversight evidence — rather than retrofitting it after CE marking.

## Bottom line: **Class III**, under Annex VIII, Rule 11, first indent.

### 1. Qualification first

It's medical device software (MDSW) under Article 2(1) and MDCG 2019-11: it performs an action on data beyond storage, archival, lossless compression or simple search, and it does so for a medical purpose (diagnosis / prediction, and informing treatment). Not an accessory — it's a device in its own right.

Implementing rule 3.3 (Annex VIII): software that drives or influences another device takes that device's class, but *"if the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right."* You've said standalone, no connection — so you go straight to Rule 11 rather than inheriting the CT scanner's class.

### 2. Rule 11 walkthrough

Rule 11, first indent: software intended to provide information used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes is **Class IIa**, *except*:

- if those decisions may cause **death or irreversible deterioration of health → Class III**
- if they may cause **serious deterioration of health or a surgical intervention → Class IIb**

Your intended purpose puts the device squarely in the "information used to take a decision" category — it says so almost verbatim. So the only question is the severity of the consequence of that decision going wrong.

The decision is *thrombectomy or not* in acute LVO stroke. Both error directions are severe and irreversible:

- **False negative / missed LVO** → thrombectomy not performed or delayed past the window → established infarct, permanent disability or death. Irreversible by definition; in LVO, time-to-reperfusion is the dominant determinant of outcome.
- **False positive** → an unnecessary intra-arterial procedure with a real risk of vessel dissection, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage and death.

That is "death or an irreversible deterioration" on the face of it. **Class III.**

Note that even the weaker limb doesn't help you: the decision is a decision to perform a *surgical intervention*, which on its own floors you at Class IIb. The irreversibility of stroke outcomes is what carries it to III.

### 3. The argument for IIb, and why I don't think it holds

The case for IIb runs: it's *triage* information, the neurointerventionalist reads the source CTA themselves, the software is adjunctive and "supports" rather than makes the decision, so the manufacturer's contribution to a bad outcome is bounded.

Two problems:

- Rule 11 contains no human-in-the-loop carve-out. MDCG 2019-11 anchors classification on the **significance of the information to the decision** and the **state of the healthcare situation** — acute LVO stroke is the paradigm critical situation, and triage information in a time-critical pathway is highly significant even when a clinician confirms it. The word "support" in your intended purpose is not a downgrade lever; Rule 11's trigger is "provide information which is **used to take** decisions."
- Real-world use of triage/notification tools is to *accelerate and route*. A false negative doesn't get caught by a human who never gets alerted to look.

Notified-body practice in this space is not perfectly uniform, and you will hear of stroke-imaging certificates sitting at IIa or IIb — often legacy positions, narrower intended purposes, or devices that stop at quantification rather than naming the treatment decision. I'd treat III as the defensible position for *this* intended purpose and confirm the classification rationale with your NB early, in writing, before you build the technical documentation around it.

### 4. What would actually change the class

Only a genuine change of intended purpose, not a rewording:

- If the output were image-processing or quantification with no linkage to a treatment decision (e.g. vessel segmentation for a clinician to interpret), Rule 11's "information for decisions" limb weakens — but you'd need to mean it, and marketing claims, labelling and UI must match.
- Dropping "to support the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy" and replacing it with something vaguer will not work: Article 7 and the NB will read your IFU, claims and actual clinical workflow together. Your current wording is honest and clinically correct — I'd keep it and accept Class III rather than engineer a downgrade.

### 5. What Class III commits you to

- **Conformity assessment**: Annex IX (full QMS + technical documentation assessment of *each* device), or Annex X + XI. Notified body mandatory.
- **Clinical investigation**: Article 61(4) presumptively requires one for Class III devices, subject to the Article 61(6) exceptions. Retrospective performance studies alone are unlikely to satisfy this — plan for a prospective study.
- **SSCP**: Summary of Safety and Clinical Performance required (Article 32), published on Eudamed.
- **PSUR**: updated annually, submitted to the NB via Eudamed (Article 86).
- **Not** subject to the Article 54 clinical evaluation consultation procedure ("scrutiny") — that's limited to Class III *implantables* and certain Class IIb active devices. Useful bit of relief.
- **PMCF** plan and evaluation report; expect the NB to want real-world performance monitoring given distribution shift across scanner vendors, protocols and sites.

### 6. Adjacent regimes you should scope now

- **EU AI Act**: if there's a machine-learning component — and there will be — this is a **high-risk AI system** under Article 6(1), because it's a product (or safety component) requiring third-party conformity assessment under the MDR, which is in Annex I Section A. For Annex I products the high-risk obligations apply from **2 August 2027**. Practically: build the AI Act technical documentation, data governance, logging and human-oversight requirements into the MDR file now rather than retrofitting, and check whether your NB is designated under both.
- **GSPR 17** (electronic programmable systems), **IEC 62304** — at Class III expect software safety class C, **ISO 14971**, **IEC 82304-1**, **IEC 62366-1** (human factors matter a lot here: alert design, failure-to-alert behaviour, degraded-mode messaging).

## Bottom line

**Class IIa under MDR Annex VIII, Rule 11** — assuming it qualifies as a medical device, which with that intended purpose it does. Class I is not credibly reachable as written, and IIb is not triggered.

## Step 1 — Does it qualify? (Art. 2(1) + MDCG 2019-11)

Yes, most likely. Two things pull it in:

- **Medical purpose:** your intended purpose names a diseased population (CKD) and a clinical use (review by a nephrologist). That is *monitoring* of disease in the Art. 2(1) sense, even though no single reading drives an acute decision.
- **Action on data:** MDCG 2019-11 excludes software that only stores, archives, communicates or does simple search. Trending is the weak point — plotting raw values is arguably close to "display only," but you are explicitly creating a weeks-long trend view for clinical interpretation, and the standalone-app framing plus the CKD indication makes the "it's just a diary" argument hard to hold in front of a notified body.

The "no alarms / not for acute decisions" facts are genuinely useful — but they affect the *class*, not whether it's a device.

## Step 2 — Rule 11

Rule 11 has two limbs, and implementing rule 3.5 means the highest applicable class wins:

| Limb | Applies? | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Information used for diagnostic/therapeutic decisions | Arguably yes — the nephrologist titrates antihypertensives / assesses fluid status off the trend | IIa (not IIb: no risk of serious deterioration or surgery from a trend reviewed at a scheduled visit; not III) |
| Monitoring of physiological processes | Yes — BP and weight over time | IIa |
| Vital physiological parameters with immediate danger → IIb | **No** | — |

BP *is* a vital physiological parameter, so the IIb carve-out is the one to argue away deliberately: once-daily self-entry, no alarms, no thresholds, no real-time surveillance, reviewed weeks later at an appointment. The nature of the variations you capture cannot produce immediate danger, because nothing in the system is intended to act on them in time. Document that reasoning explicitly in your classification rationale — it's the load-bearing argument for IIa over IIb.

Note that Rule 11's "all other software is Class I" catch-all is, in practice, nearly empty. Anything that monitors a physiological process lands in IIa at minimum.

## If you want out of MDR scope entirely

That's the only realistic route to "no notified body," and it means committing to a genuinely non-medical product:

- Reframe the intended purpose as a general wellbeing/self-tracking log with no named condition, no clinical-review claim, and no mention of nephrology.
- No CKD-specific content, no reference ranges, no colour-coding, no "normal/high" labels, no derived metrics (MAP, dry-weight deltas, rate-of-change), no clinician-facing export framed as a clinical record.
- Accept that you cannot market it to nephrology clinics or claim it supports consultations.

If any of those constraints is unacceptable to the product, stop trying and plan for IIa.

## Practical consequences of IIa

Notified body involvement (Annex IX Ch. I+III, or Annex XI), a full QMS to ISO 13485, IEC 62304 software lifecycle, ISO 14971 risk management, IEC 62366 usability, clinical evaluation under Art. 61 + MDCG 2020-1 (performance data for an MDSW like this, not a full trial), PMS/PMCF, UDI and EUDAMED registration. Budget the notified body lead time — that's usually the schedule driver, not the engineering.

One thing worth pinning down early: whether the nephrologist-facing view is part of the same device or a separate clinician product, since that affects your intended-purpose wording and the usability/human-factors work for two distinct user groups.

This is my read of the regulation and MDCG guidance, not a substitute for a regulatory consultant's sign-off on the classification rationale you'll file.

**Class IIa under Rule 11 — *if* it qualifies as a medical device at all.** The real question in your case isn't the class, it's the qualification step, and your intended purpose sits right on the line.

## Step 1: Does it qualify as MDSW?

MDCG 2019-11 decision step 3 asks whether the software performs an action on data **beyond** storage, archival, communication, simple search, or lossless compression.

Your app does two things:
- **Records** patient-entered values → clearly just storage/communication → not MDSW on its own (this is the "electronic patient diary / EHR-type" case).
- **Trends** them over weeks → this is where it turns. Plotting stored values on a time axis is arguably pure *presentation* of data the patient already entered, creating no new medical information. That reading keeps you out of scope.

Arguments that push it **into** scope:
- Your intended purpose names a patient population (CKD) and a clinical use context (nephrology consultation), so the action is plainly "for the benefit of individual patients" and has a medical purpose — monitoring of a chronic disease. MDCG 2019-11 treats software intended to monitor physiological parameters as MDSW even when the computation is trivial.
- Weight and BP in CKD are specifically the inputs for fluid-status and antihypertensive management. "Trend for review by the nephrologist" is, functionally, information feeding a therapeutic decision.

In my judgement, a notified body or competent authority reviewing this would more likely than not call it MDSW. The absence of alarms and acute use reduces the *class*, not the *qualification*.

## Step 2: Classification (Annex VIII, Rule 11)

Assuming MDSW, Rule 11 applies (standalone software is classified in its own right under implementing rule 3.3; it isn't an accessory since no device is driven or influenced):

- **¶1 — information used for diagnostic/therapeutic decisions → IIa**, escalating to IIb/III by harm severity. The nephrologist adjusting fluid or BP management on the trend is a therapeutic decision. Escalation to IIb ("serious deterioration or surgical intervention") is not supportable for a trend reviewed at a scheduled visit with no acute role — so **IIa**.
- **¶2 — monitoring of physiological processes → IIa**, escalating to IIb only where variations in *vital* physiological parameters "could result in immediate danger". Blood pressure is a vital parameter, but once-daily home entry with no alarms and no acute decision fails the immediate-danger test. So again **IIa**, not IIb.
- **¶3 — "all other software" → Class I.** This is a narrow catch-all in practice; it's hard to sustain once you've accepted the software both monitors and informs decisions.

So: **IIa**, which means notified body involvement, Annex IX or XI conformity assessment, and full QMS certification — a materially different burden from Class I self-declaration.

## The lever you actually have

The gap between "out of scope" and "Class IIa" here is your claims, not your code. To hold a non-device position you would need to:

- Keep the intended purpose to recording and displaying patient-entered data, and drop language that reads as clinical monitoring of CKD.
- Add **no** interpretation layer whatsoever: no reference ranges, no normal/high colour coding, no fitted trend lines or slope figures, no flags, no summary statistics presented as clinically meaningful, no thresholds.
- Ensure marketing, screenshots, and app-store text match — claims material is assessed alongside the IFU, and this is where most "we're just a diary" positions collapse.
- Document the qualification rationale explicitly against the MDCG 2019-11 decision steps and keep it in your technical file, so the position is defensible rather than assumed.

Note that "trend" in your current intended-purpose wording is the single riskiest word. If you mean a plain time-series chart, say so; if you mean anything computed, you're in IIa.

Two things that would change the answer: adding any alarm or threshold alert on BP would open the IIb question under Rule 11 ¶2, and any use in acute or between-visit decision-making would strengthen the ¶1 path and could push escalation. Separately, if you're also targeting Great Britain, UKCA still runs on the pre-MDR rules, where this would very likely be Class I — don't assume the EU answer transfers.

As described, I'd argue this is **not a medical device under the MDR at all** — so no class. If you concede device status (or if your claims drift), the fallback is **Rule 11 → Class IIa**. Class I is hard to reach once Rule 11 bites.

## Why it falls outside

MDCG 2019-11's decision path is the relevant test. Step 3 asks whether the software performs an action on data *beyond* storage, archival, communication, simple search, or lossless compression. Your app:

- takes values the patient reads off their own (separately CE-marked) cuff and scale,
- stores them,
- plots them on a time axis.

No derived indices, no reference-range flags, no alarms, no algorithmic output. The nephrologist supplies all the interpretation. That's an electronic diary, in the same family as EHR/HIS functionality that the guidance places out of scope.

The exposure is almost entirely in wording and feature creep:

- **"Trend" is your riskiest word.** If a reader takes it to mean the app computes a direction, slope, rate of weight gain, or averages (MAP, 7-day mean), you've created new medical information → MDSW → Rule 11 → **Class IIa** (notified body, QMS, clinical evaluation). Write and sign a **borderline/qualification rationale** that walks MDCG 2019-11 Figure 1 step by step and records the "no interpretation, no alarms, no acute use" boundary as a design constraint, not just a current fact. ## Short answer: **Class I** (Rule 11, final limb — "all other software")

### How you get there under Annex VIII

**Step 1 — Implementing rule 3.3.** "Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device. If the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right." Your product is standalone and doesn't drive or influence the modality, the PACS, or the reporting workstation, so it is classified on its own intended purpose, not by inheritance.

**Step 2 — Rule 11 is the applicable rule** (it is the software-specific rule, and implementing rule 3.5 means the strictest applicable rule governs — here no other limb of Rule 11 or other rule bites):

| Rule 11 limb | Applies? |
|---|---|
| Software providing information *used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes* → IIa (IIb / III if serious harm, death or irreversible deterioration) | **No** — the diagnostic information is generated and signed by the clinician *before* the software touches it. The software contributes no new information, no interpretation, no prioritisation, no flagging. It performs transport and presentation only. |
| Software intended to monitor physiological processes → IIa (IIb for vital parameters with immediate danger) | No |
| **All other software → Class I** | **Yes** |

**Step 3 — Class I sub-category.** Not sterile, not a measuring function, not a reusable surgical instrument → plain **Class I**, i.e. self-certification under Article 52(7): Annex II + III technical documentation, your own Declaration of Conformity, **no notified body**. ## The reasoning through Annex VIII

**Rule 11, first limb** — software "intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes" → Class IIa (IIb/III on severity). The question is whether *your* software provides that information, or merely moves it.

On your stated facts it does not provide it in the Rule 11 sense:

- The diagnostic information is created, interpreted and signed by the radiologist **before** the software touches it.
- The software performs no analysis, no interpretation, no calculation, no modification of clinical content, and adds nothing.
- Its function is presentation-layer transformation plus transmission. That is the same functional category MDCG 2019-11 treats as data communication/storage/lossless reformatting.

**Rule 11, second limb** — monitoring of physiological processes: not applicable, nothing is monitored.

**Rule 11, third limb** — "all other software" → **Class I**.

**Implementing rule 3.3** — the software is standalone, not driving or influencing another device, so it does not inherit a class from hardware. **Rule 3.5** (strictest applicable rule) changes nothing, since no other rule bites. Rule 13's active-device catch-all would also land on Class I.

Note that under MDR, Class I means self-certification under Art. 52(7) — no notified body — provided it is not Im (measuring), Is (sterile) or Ir (reusable surgical), none of which apply.

## The contestable point, stated plainly

There is a real argument the other way that you should expect to have to rebut. A reviewer can say: the GP reads the report *in the layout your software produced*, and uses it to make diagnostic and therapeutic decisions — therefore the software "provides information used to take decisions," Rule 11 first limb, **Class IIa**.

The counter-argument, which I think is the stronger one, is that Rule 11 targets software whose *own* output contributes information to the decision. Reading it otherwise would pull every PACS, RIS, DICOM router, HL7 interface engine and hospital mail gateway into Class IIa, which is not how Rule 11 has been applied.

Because it's standalone, the Annex VIII Chapter II implementing rule for software applies: software independent of any other device *"shall be classified in its own right"* — so you classify the programme itself, not some parent hardware. That lands you in Rule 11 (Annex VIII, Ch. III, 6.3), and the first sub‑rule gives **Class IIa**.

## Why not Class I

Your framing — no clinician in the loop, doesn't feed information to anyone to decide anything, *it is the treatment* — is exactly the argument for the Rule 11 catch‑all (*"all other software is classified as class I"*). It's a coherent reading of the text, and I'd expect a notified body to reject it.

Rule 11's trigger is software *"intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes."* MDCG 2019‑11 is explicit that the decision‑maker can be a healthcare professional **or the patient / lay person**. Your product tells the patient to be in bed from 00:40 to 05:40, to get out of bed after 20 minutes awake, to re‑appraise a specific belief. The patient then acts. That is information driving a therapeutic decision, and the decision is algorithmically derived from their diary data.

So removing the clinician doesn't remove the decision — it removes the *mitigation*. A prescription DTx for a diagnosed chronic condition, self‑certified with no notified body, is a conspicuous target for a competent authority, and a forced reclassification after launch is far more expensive than starting at IIa. Note also that IIa doesn't shut doors: BfArM's DiGA fast‑track accepts Class I and IIa alike.

## Why not IIb or III

Rule 11 escalates on the consequence of the decision: IIb for serious deterioration or a surgical intervention, III for death or irreversible deterioration. Sleep restriction does have a genuine harm pathway — acute sleep debt causing daytime impairment and motor‑vehicle risk, lowered seizure threshold, mania induction in bipolar disorder. You should expect to be asked about it, and answer it in the technical file rather than leave it implicit:

- a time‑in‑bed floor (commonly 5–5.5 h) so titration can't run away;
- contraindication screening at onboarding — bipolar disorder, seizure disorders, untreated OSA, occupational drivers/shift workers;
- explicit driving and machinery warnings during the restriction phase.

These are Annex I risk controls, not classification arguments, but they're what makes the IIa position hold rather than drift toward IIb.

## One alternative reading to pre‑empt

Because the strictest applicable rule wins, your rationale should close off **Rule 22** (active therapeutic device with an integrated diagnostic function that significantly determines patient management — closed‑loop systems, AEDs → Class III). Software is an active device under Art. 2(4), and an algorithm that reads sleep diary data and re‑titrates the prescription each week is superficially closed‑loop. The distinction to state plainly: the input is patient self‑report, not an integrated diagnostic measurement, and nothing is delivered to the patient automatically — every step is mediated by the patient's own action. **Rule 11** then has exactly three limbs, and you have to fail the first two to land in the third:

1. *Software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes* → IIa, escalating to IIb (serious deterioration / surgical intervention) or III (death / irreversible deterioration). **Not engaged**, on your stated intended purpose: the software administers the therapy itself. It is not generating output that a decision-taker consumes in order to decide something.
2. *Software intended to monitor physiological processes* → IIa, or IIb for vital physiological parameters. **Not engaged.** A sleep diary is patient-reported data collected to run the protocol; it isn't monitoring of a physiological process in the Rule 11 sense, and sleep continuity is not a vital physiological parameter.
3. **All other software → Class I.** This is your bucket. Therapeutic software that *is* the intervention has no dedicated rule in Annex VIII and falls here.

**Cross-checks:** Rule 12 (administering or removing medicinal products, body fluids, energy) doesn't apply. Rule 22 (active therapeutic device with integrated diagnostic function that significantly determines patient management — closed-loop systems, AEDs) doesn't apply: there's no diagnostic function. Rule 13 ("all other active devices") would also give Class I, so implementing rule 3.5 (highest applicable class) changes nothing.

Note that "prescription-only" has no bearing on MDR classification — unlike the US, where prescription status is a regulatory control in its own right. Here it affects only labelling and IFU obligations under Annex I §23.

## The pressure point you should expect

Rule 11's first limb is the contested one, and the sleep restriction module is where a notified body or competent authority will push. Two facts work against your "doesn't feed information to anyone to decide anything" framing:

- MDCG 2019-11 is explicit that the decision-taker under Rule 11 can be the **patient or a lay user**, not only a clinician. So "no clinician in the loop" does not by itself take you out of limb 1.
- Sleep restriction scheduling takes diary input and computes a **personalised** time-in-bed prescription that the patient then acts on. Read aggressively, that output is information used to take a therapeutic decision. Read properly — and I think correctly — it is the delivery of the therapy in the same way a titration protocol executed by the device is not decision support.

If limb 1 were held to apply, the next question is impact severity, and the plausible argument for escalation is that induced sleep deprivation causes daytime somnolence and therefore road-traffic or occupational accident risk. That's the route to a IIb argument. I don't think it survives contact with the actual evidence base for CBT-I, but it's the argument that gets made.

**Precedent is on your side.** CBT-I and CBT-based digital therapeutics have generally been CE-marked Class I in the EU — Sleepio, somnio, and deprexis are the usual reference points. Verify current status in EUDAMED yourself rather than relying on my recollection, but the regulatory practice is well established.

**How to protect the Class I position:** write the intended purpose and the IFU so the software is unambiguously the treatment, and keep three things out of the product unless you're prepared to re-classify:

- Any diagnostic, screening, or triage output — ISI or PSQI scoring presented as an assessment, or comorbidity flagging for sleep apnoea, depression, or suicidality. Safety screening is clinically desirable and pushes you straight into limb 1, so build it as a hard stop referring out rather than as a scored assessment surfaced to the user.
- Any clinician-facing dashboard or report intended to inform treatment decisions.
- Wearable-derived sleep metrics presented with accuracy claims — that risks both limb 2 and a measuring function (Class Im), which drags in a notified body for metrological aspects even at Class I.

- Annex II/III technical documentation; GSPR checklist against Annex I (including §17 on electronic programmable systems)

## Bottom line

**Class IIa, MDR Annex VIII Rule 11 (first limb).** That's where I'd classify it and what I'd defend in the technical documentation. Your Class I argument is real and I'll set it out below, but I wouldn't build a regulatory strategy on it.

## The rule path

- **Implementing Rule 3.3 (Annex VIII):** the software is independent of any other device, so it is classified in its own right — not by reference to a hardware parent.
- **Software is an active device**, so Rules 9–13 and 22 are in scope. Rule 9 doesn't bite (no administration or exchange of energy). Rule 10 doesn't bite (not diagnosis/monitoring hardware). Rule 22 doesn't bite (no closed-loop therapy delivery with integrated diagnostics).
- **Rule 11** is therefore the operative rule, and Implementing Rule 3.5 means the strictest applicable reading governs.

## Why IIa rather than I

Your position is that the software *is* the therapy, not information feeding someone's decision — so Rule 11's first limb is not engaged and you fall to its residual sentence, "all other software is classified as class I." That is a coherent literal reading of the text.

The problem is MDCG 2019-11 Rev.1, which reads "used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes" broadly and is explicit that the decision-maker may be **the patient or a lay person**, not only a healthcare professional. On that reading your product does provide such information: a prescribed sleep window ("be in bed 00:30–06:00"), stimulus-control instructions, and restructuring exercises are outputs the patient acts on therapeutically. A notified body or competent authority will almost certainly take that view, and the absence of a clinician in the loop cuts *against* you here — there is no professional filter between the software's output and the patient's behaviour.

Practically: most Class I CBT-I and DTx CE marks you'll find are legacy MDD marks. Under MDR, patient-facing therapeutic software has consistently been pulled into IIa. Self-certifying a *prescription* therapeutic as Class I is the kind of claim that gets challenged — and Article 51(2) lets a competent authority refer the classification to the Commission for a binding decision. Being re-classified after launch is far more expensive than starting at IIa: Annex IX conformity assessment, notified body queue, no grandfathering of your clinical evidence format.

## What could push it to IIb — address this deliberately

Rule 11 escalates to IIb where the decision may cause "serious deterioration of a person's state of health." There are three arguments a reviewer can make against CBT-I:

1. **Sleep restriction lowers the seizure threshold** in people with epilepsy.
2. **Sleep restriction can precipitate mania or hypomania** in bipolar disorder.
3. **Iatrogenic daytime sleepiness** during the restriction phase → road traffic or occupational accident.

IIa holds if — and only if — your intended purpose, contraindications, in-app screening/exclusion criteria, and safety instructions handle these explicitly and your risk management file shows it. If any of that is thin, expect a IIb challenge. The third argument is also the seed of a (weak, remote-causation) Class III argument; it's normally rejected, but don't leave it unaddressed.

## Two things to confirm

- **Does the product ingest sensor data — actigraphy, wearable, phone-based sleep staging?** Your description implies self-reported sleep diaries only. Self-report is not "monitoring physiological processes"; continuous sensor-derived sleep monitoring plausibly is, engaging Rule 11's second limb. That limb is also IIa, so it doesn't change the outcome, but it changes the rationale you write down and your clinical evaluation obligations.
- **Prescription status is irrelevant to classification.** It affects labelling and supply, not Rule 11. Don't let it appear in the classification rationale as though it mitigates risk.

## Suggested rationale wording for the technical documentation

> The device is MDSW independent of any other device (Annex VIII, Implementing Rule 3.3) and is classified in its own right. It is an active device providing information — individualised sleep-scheduling parameters and behavioural/cognitive instructions — which the patient uses to take decisions with a therapeutic purpose. Rule 11, first limb, applies: **Class IIa**. Escalation to Class IIb is not warranted because identified hazards associated with sleep restriction (seizure threshold reduction, affective switch in bipolar disorder, transient daytime sleepiness) are controlled by intended-purpose limitation, stated contraindications, pre-enrolment screening and in-programme safety instructions, such that residual risk does not extend to serious deterioration of health or surgical intervention. Rules 9, 10 and 22 do not apply (no administration or exchange of energy; no diagnostic or monitoring hardware function; no closed-loop delivery).

If you want to pursue Class I anyway, the decision point is whether you're prepared to argue "therapy delivery is not information provision" to a competent authority without a notified body behind you. I'd get that reading pressure-tested by regulatory counsel before it goes into your declaration of conformity — and I'd plan the QMS and clinical evaluation to IIa standard regardless, so a re-classification is a paperwork event rather than a rebuild.

Short answer: **no, not on the facts as you've stated them** — pure retrieval falls inside an explicit carve-out. But the carve-out is narrower than people assume, and the line is drawn exactly at the "adds value" point you're asking about.

## The authority

**MDCG 2019-11** — *Guidance on Qualification and Classification of Software in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR) and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (IVDR)*, Medical Device Coordination Group, October 2019 (a Rev. 1 has since been issued — pull the current PDF from the Commission's MDCG page rather than an older cached copy).

The operative provision is **Decision step 3** of the qualification flowchart (Figure 1):

> Is the software performing an action on data different from storage, archival, communication, *simple search* or lossless compression?

If the answer is no, the software is **not MDSW**. Your tool answers no.

The accompanying note is the part you actually want, because it defines both sides of the line (wording is close to verbatim — worth confirming character-for-character against the PDF before it goes in a file):

> "'Simple search' refers to the retrieval of records by matching record metadata against record search criteria or to the retrieval of information. … Simple search does **not** include software which provides interpretative search results, e.g. to identify medical findings in health records or turn unstructured search results into value (e.g. to identify, analyse or diagnose)."

Supporting cites if you need to build the argument out:

- **MDR Recital 19** — software qualifies as a device only when *specifically intended by the manufacturer* for a medical purpose; "software for general purposes, even when used in a healthcare setting" does not.
- **MDR Article 2(1)** — the intended-purpose definition itself.
- **MDCG 2019-11** also treats Hospital Information Systems as generally outside scope where they store, archive and transfer patient data for patient-management support. A document library search sits comfortably in that company.

## Where it flips

The exclusion is about what the software *does to the data*, so these are the tripwires:

- **Relevance ranking or scoring** — you've said you don't, and that's the right call. Ordering results by clinical relevance is arguably "turning unstructured search results into value."
- **Semantic / embedding-based retrieval, snippet generation, summarisation of hits** — all interpretative. Note that "we use vectors instead of keywords" is a qualification-relevant change, not just an implementation detail.
- **Patient-context filtering** — the moment results are narrowed using *this patient's* data, you're likely through Decision step 4 (action for the benefit of individual patients) as well.
- **Intended purpose as marketed.** This is the one that bites hardest. Qualification follows your claims, not your architecture. "Search the document library" is safe. "Helps clinicians find the right protocol for their patient" is a medical-purpose claim, and your IFU, marketing copy and sales deck are all evidence of intended purpose.

Full-text matching on document *body* text (rather than metadata only) is a mild grey edge against the literal wording, but exact-match full-text search is the library-catalogue case the note is describing. I wouldn't lose sleep over it.

## Two things you didn't ask but probably need

**Jurisdiction.** The above is EU. If this is also US-facing, the reasoning is different but lands in the same place: FD&C Act **§520(o)(1)(B)** (added by the 21st Century Cures Act) excludes software for transferring, storing, converting formats and displaying data, and §520(o)(1)(A) covers EHR-type records. FDA's *Clinical Decision Support Software* guidance (September 2022) is the one to read if you ever add ranking. UK is MHRA's stand-alone software guidance, which tracks the MDCG position.

**Article 5(5) MDR.** "Our hospital's document library" reads like you may be a health institution building in-house. If so, the in-house exemption may be in play as a fallback — but it carries its own conditions (no transfer to another legal entity, documented justification, QMS-equivalent requirements). It's a worse position than simply not being a device, so lead with the Decision step 3 argument and keep 5(5) in reserve.

I'd write the Decision step 3 analysis into your technical file / qualification rationale now, while the "no scoring, no ranking" design decision is fresh — it's much cheaper than reconstructing it later, and it gives you a documented baseline to diff against when someone proposes adding relevance ranking in six months.

The "adds value" line you're asking about is drawn in the footnote defining the term:

> "'Simple search' refers to the retrieval of records by matching record metadata against record search criteria, e.g. library functions. Simple search does not cover software which provides interpretative search results, e.g. to identify medical findings in health records or based on the analysis of medical images."

So the statutory line is **interpretation, not effort**. Matching a query against document metadata and content and returning hits = library function. Deriving a *finding* — "these are the documents relevant to this patient's condition," "this image shows X" — is interpretative and puts you back in the tree.

Supporting: **MDR Recital 19** (software is a device only when *specifically intended* by the manufacturer for a medical purpose; general-purpose software used in a healthcare setting is not), and MDCG 2019-11's treatment of Hospital Information Systems, which are not MDSW when they support the care process by storing, archiving and retrieving.

## Other jurisdictions

- **UK**: MHRA, *Medical device stand-alone software including apps*. Mirrors the MDCG decision logic and the same simple-search exclusion under UK MDR 2002.
- **US**: your tool most likely doesn't meet the device definition at all. If anyone pushes back, the fallback is FD&C Act **§520(o)(1)(E)** (added by the 21st Century Cures Act) and FDA's **Clinical Decision Support Software** final guidance (September 2022) — note that the §520(o)(1)(E) safe harbour is narrower than people assume, so lead with "not a device," not with CDS.

Worth writing these into your design constraints, because each one is a re-classification event, not a feature tweak:

1. **LLM-generated answers, summaries or synthesised snippets** over the retrieved docs. This is the big one — that's plainly "an action on data" beyond retrieval.
2. **Ranking by clinical relevance.** Lexical/BM25 relevance ordering is still matching query against content. "Best guideline for this patient" is a finding.
3. **Patient-context-aware retrieval** — auto-pulling documents off the open patient record rather than off a typed query.
4. **The intended purpose you publish.** This is where teams actually lose the argument. Qualification is driven by the manufacturer's stated intended purpose, so marketing copy saying "surfaces the right protocol for your patient" can qualify a product that the code alone would not. ## Bottom line

As described — matching a query against an existing document library and returning the matching documents, nothing more — **that is not Medical Device Software under EU MDR.** It falls out at the "simple search" carve-out. But the carve-out is narrow and the boundary is exactly where you've drawn it, so the description has to stay true.

## The authority (EU)

**MDCG 2019-11**, *Guidance on Qualification and Classification of Software in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 – MDR and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 – IVDR* (Oct 2019, since revised as Rev. 1 — check the Commission's MDCG page, the section numbering shifted between versions).

The operative test is **Decision Step 3** of its qualification flowchart:

> Is the software performing an action on data different from storage, archival, communication, simple search or lossless compression?

If no → not MDSW. Pure retrieval answers "no."

The guidance then defines the term, and this is the sentence you actually want to cite:

> **Simple search** refers to the retrieval of records by matching record metadata against record search criteria, e.g. library functions.
>
> Simple search **does not cover** software which provides interpretative search results, e.g. to identify medical findings in health records or medical literature.

That second sentence *is* the official position on "simple search vs. search that adds value." The line is **interpretation**, not sophistication. Retrieval = out of scope. Anything that tells the clinician which results matter clinically = in scope.

Supporting: **MDR Recital 19** (software qualifies only where the manufacturer specifically intends a medical purpose; general-purpose software used in healthcare does not) and **Article 2(1)**. MDCG 2019-11 also confirms Hospital Information Systems and EHR software are not devices where they only store/archive/communicate.

If it ever *did* qualify, **Rule 11, Annex VIII MDR** would put it at **Class IIa** minimum — information used to take diagnostic or therapeutic decisions. That's the size of the cliff you're standing next to.

## US and UK, briefly

- **US:** FD&C Act **§520(o)(1)(C)** (added by the 21st Century Cures Act) excludes software limited to transferring, storing, converting formats, or displaying data — *unless* it interprets or analyses. **§520(o)(1)(E)** is the CDS exclusion, and prong (ii) expressly contemplates displaying "peer-reviewed clinical studies and clinical practice guidelines," which is squarely your use case. See FDA's **Clinical Decision Support Software** guidance (final, Sept 2022). Note FDA reads the CDS exclusion narrowly — in particular it treats prioritising or ranking options as falling outside it.
- **UK:** MHRA's *Medical device stand-alone software including apps* guidance follows the same qualification logic under UK MDR 2002.

## What would flip it

Worth pressure-testing before you rely on this:

1. **Intended purpose beats technical function.** If marketing, labelling, or the UI says anything like "find the right protocol for this patient," you've claimed a medical purpose and the code doesn't save you.
2. **Ranking.** You say there's none. Plain text-relevance ordering (BM25/TF-IDF) is defensible as simple search; *clinical* relevance ranking is not. Keep them clearly separable.
3. **Semantic/embedding search.** MDCG's wording is "matching record metadata against record search criteria." Vector similarity over document content is a harder argument than keyword matching — not automatically fatal, but not obviously covered either.
4. **Snippets or summaries.** The moment you generate an answer, extract, or abstract rather than return the document, that's creating or modifying medical information. Straight to in-scope.
5. **Auto-populating the query from the patient record.** That starts to engage Decision Step 4 (action for the benefit of an individual patient).

Write the qualification rationale down now, mapped to the Step 3 wording, and re-run it each time someone proposes a feature. That document is what a competent authority or notified body will ask for, and "we never ranked anything" is much easier to defend with a dated record than from memory.
